title: Weight Gain, Bruising, Purple Striae / Ask About Every Capsule Before You Test

blocks.text: Weight Gain, Bruising, Purple Striae / Ask About Every Capsule Before You Test

AMaC MRCP PACES · X-05 · Consultation · PACES Consultation (Station 5) · Skills A, B, C, D, E, F, G · 20 minutes (15 with the patient, then 5 of examiner questions; warning at 13 minutes) · Guidelines: Endocrine Society clinical practice guideline: The diagnosis of Cushing's syndrome (J Clin Endocrinol Metab 2008;93:1526-40); ESE and Endocrine Society joint guideline on glucocorticoid-induced adrenal insufficiency (J Clin Endocrinol Metab 2024) · Related AMaC: None identified

Dear Doctor, a 38-year-old hairdresser. Eight months of weight gain, easy bruising, purple stretch marks and weak legs. Newly raised blood pressure and HbA1c. Combined oral contraceptive pill. Please assess and advise.
The patient has consented to see you. Please take a history, perform a relevant examination and explain your assessment and plan to the patient.

sections.heading: 4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap

blocks.text: The Hook. A round face, purple striae, bruising and proximal weakness is Cushing's syndrome until the cause is found. The first step is not a test: it is to ask about every steroid she takes, because a drug is a recognised cause.

The Examiner Trap. She is embarrassed and has been taking herbal capsules for her joints. Candidates order a pituitary scan before asking. Pass: ask about all products, exclude exogenous steroid, then test. Fail: scan first, or stop the capsules abruptly.

rows: Think
Say
Do
Ask about the changes, then ask about every pill, capsule, cream and injection, including herbal and online products.
"What do you take for your joints or skin? Anything from a market, shop or website? Are you on the pill?"
Weight; bruising; striae; weakness; mood; sleep; periods; hair; steroids; contraceptive pill; infections; fractures.
Look for the discriminating features and check blood pressure and strength.
"May I look at your face and skin, check your blood pressure, and see how strong your thighs are? Tell me if anything hurts."
Face; fat pads; striae; bruises; thin skin; proximal myopathy; blood pressure; fundi; cover her.
Explain what you suspect, why you will ask about the capsules first, and the safe plan.
"I think a steroid is raising your cortisol. Don't stop the capsules suddenly; we'll plan that safely and test your own hormones."
Exclude exogenous; stop safely; steroid card; tests; bone, sugar, pressure; follow-up.

blocks.text: High-performance is an AMaC teaching label, not an official grade. It shows what lifts a pass from adequate to convincing. Critical fail is an AMaC practice flag for an action that could harm the patient today; it is not an official automatic PACES fail.
Who you are: A 38-year-old hairdresser. You are self-conscious about your appearance and polite, and you do not want to be told off.
Opening line: "I've put on loads of weight, I bruise at the slightest bump and I've got these purple lines on my tummy. I can't climb the stairs at work without holding on."
Volunteered: eight months. Mood low and tearful. Periods irregular.

Only if asked what you take: the combined contraceptive pill. Nothing else prescribed. Never smoked; alcohol a few glasses at weekends; no allergies; no recent travel. Your mother has type 2 diabetes. You live with your partner.

Only if asked specifically about herbal products or anything from shops or websites: eight months ago you started "joint relief" capsules from a market stall, two daily, for aching hands. They helped at once and you do not want to stop.

Hidden concern (only if asked what worries you): you are afraid you have a brain tumour, and ashamed that you took capsules you could not name. Say: "I'm scared you'll take them away and the pain will come back."
Your questions, in your own words: "Is it a brain tumour?" "Do I have to stop the capsules?" "Will my body go back?"
How you react: if lectured, you stop talking. If listened to and given a clear safe plan, you agree. If told to stop the capsules at once, you refuse. If offered options, you choose.

Findings, released when examined: comfortable; pulse 84 regular; blood pressure 156/96; temperature 36.7 °C. Round face; plethora; central obesity; supraclavicular fat pads; thin skin with bruises; purple striae on the abdomen and thighs. Proximal myopathy: cannot rise from a chair without arms. No pigmentation. Fundi normal.
Results, only when requested: HbA1c in the diabetic range; potassium low-normal; ACTH suppressed; late-night salivary cortisol low; DXA: low bone density. Capsule analysis (if sent): prednisolone.

Question ladder: 1. What is your first step? (E) Exclude exogenous glucocorticoid. 2. Diagnosis? (D) 3. Which tests for endogenous Cushing's syndrome? (E) 4. How could the pill mislead you? (E) 5. How do you stop it safely? (E)
Curveballs: She asks to stop the capsules today: no, adrenal crisis risk. She is vomiting and faint: urgent hydrocortisone. She asks whether she needs brain surgery: no, not for an exogenous cause.
Introduces self, asks consent and asks about discomfort before examining (G)
Asks about every pill, capsule, cream and online product, and the contraceptive pill (C)
Checks blood pressure, bruising, striae and proximal strength (A)
Finds moon face, fat pads, striae and proximal myopathy (B)
Names exogenous Cushing's syndrome as the first diagnosis to exclude (D)
Excludes exogenous steroid before testing, then names salivary, urinary or dexamethasone tests (E)
Says oestrogen can raise cortisol-binding globulin and confuse tests (E)
Says do not stop suddenly; taper under supervision with a steroid card (E)
Gives urgent warning signs: vomiting, faintness, infection (E)
Asks what worries her, and answers without judgement (F)

Examiner note: Critical fail (AMaC practice flag, not an official automatic PACES fail): stopping a steroid abruptly after months can cause an adrenal crisis. No consent, no capsule history, obesity assumed, and she was lectured.
Pass performance

CANDIDATE: I'm the registrar. May I check your face and skin, your blood pressure and your thigh strength? Tell me if anything hurts. I'll cover you afterwards, and thank you for letting me examine you. [R1 Pass]

CANDIDATE: Tell me about the weight, bruising, stretch marks, weak legs, mood and periods. What do you take for your joints? Any tablets, capsules or creams, or anything from a shop or website? [R2 Pass]
PATIENT: Capsules from a market stall, for eight months. And the pill.
CANDIDATE: (Examines.) Moon face, bruises, purple striae, weak thighs, raised blood pressure. [R3 Pass]
CANDIDATE: The capsules may contain a steroid, so this may be exogenous Cushing's. [R4 Pass]
CANDIDATE: First I exclude a steroid; then salivary cortisol or a dexamethasone test, which the pill can mislead. [R5 Pass]
CANDIDATE: Don't stop suddenly; we'll taper under supervision. Carry a steroid card. Vomiting, faintness or infection needs urgent help. [R6 Pass]
CANDIDATE: What worries you? [R7 Pass]
PATIENT: A brain tumour, and the pain coming back.
CANDIDATE: Both are fair, and I'm not judging you. [R7 Pass] We can plan the taper with tests, or test first. Which do you prefer? [R8 Pass]
Examiner note: Asked about every product, protected her from an abrupt stop and gave a safety net. Did not name other causes or treat the blood pressure and glucose.
High-performance performance
CANDIDATE: I'm the registrar. May I examine you? Would you like a chaperone? I'll ask before looking at your abdomen and thighs. [R1 High]
CANDIDATE: Any fractures, infections, steroid courses before, or who supplied the capsules? [R2 High]
CANDIDATE: (Examines.) Supraclavicular fat pads, no pigmentation, normal fundi. [R3 High]
CANDIDATE: Exogenous glucocorticoid Cushing's; pituitary, adrenal and ectopic causes follow only if the steroid is excluded. Depression can confuse tests. [R4 High]
CANDIDATE: Exclude steroid, then two salivary or urinary cortisols, ACTH, HbA1c, lipids, potassium and DXA. Oestrogen raises cortisol-binding globulin. [R5 High]

CANDIDATE: Supervised taper, steroid card, capsules sent for analysis, treatment for blood pressure, glucose and bones, and a review of the combined pill because of your blood pressure and clot risk. [R6 High]
CANDIDATE: Body changes can improve once the steroid is stopped safely. [R7 High]
CANDIDATE: I'll give you written steroid advice and review you with results. [R8 High]
Examiner note: Added a chaperone, wider history, other causes, test interference, capsule analysis, treating complications and a written plan.
R2: Not asking about herbal products. The capsules are the cause, and they are admitted only when asked directly.
R5: Ordering an MRI first. Exogenous steroid must be excluded before any pituitary search.
R6: Stopping the capsules at once. After months of exposure, her own adrenals are suppressed.
R7: Lecturing her. She will hide the capsules and the tablets, and the diagnosis is delayed.
"Can I check every capsule, cream and injection you use, including from shops?"
"I should exclude a steroid before I order any test."
"I'd like to check I've understood what worries you most."

Endocrine Society 2008: take a thorough drug history first to exclude exogenous glucocorticoid. Initial tests, choose one: at least two urinary free cortisols, two late-night salivary cortisols, a 1 mg overnight dexamethasone test, or the longer low-dose test.

A post-dexamethasone cortisol above 50 nmol/litre suggests Cushing's. Oestrogens raise cortisol-binding globulin and may cause false positives, and about half of women on oral contraceptives may have false-positive overnight tests.

Conditions that raise cortisol without Cushing's: depression, alcohol dependence, poorly controlled diabetes, morbid obesity and pregnancy. While she is still taking prednisolone, tests of her own cortisol axis are unreliable; the capsule analysis and a suppressed ACTH point to an exogenous source. Hypertension and a raised clot risk also mean the combined pill needs review. After long-term glucocorticoid exposure the ESE and Endocrine Society 2024 guideline advises a gradual taper towards a physiological dose, assumes adrenal insufficiency when exogenous Cushing's features are present, and advises stress-dose cover and a steroid emergency card.
THINK: Moon face, striae, myopathy: Cushing's; drug first.
SAY: "A steroid may be raising your cortisol."
DO: Ask about every capsule; test proximal strength.
NUMBERS: 1 mg DST: cortisol above 50 nmol/litre (ES 2008).
TRAP: MRI first; stopping the capsules suddenly.
FINISH: Supervised taper, steroid card, treat complications.

The diagnosis of Cushing's syndrome: an Endocrine Society clinical practice guideline (J Clin Endocrinol Metab 2008;93:1526-40). https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2386281 Supports: Excluding exogenous steroid, who to test, initial tests, the 1 mg cut-off and drug interference.

Beuschlein F et al. European Society of Endocrinology and Endocrine Society joint clinical guideline: diagnosis and therapy of glucocorticoid-induced adrenal insufficiency. J Clin Endocrinol Metab 2024 (June 2024). https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11180513/ Supports: taper after long-term glucocorticoid exposure, adrenal insufficiency assumed with exogenous Cushing's features, stress-dose and sick-day rules.
